extracted.intended_audience: medical researchers, physicians, and scientific congress participants
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for conducting, presenting, and evaluating medical scientific research and for productive participation in large scientific congresses; emphasizes observation, diversity of minds, specialization versus unity, and ethical responsibility. Also includes standards for interpreting demographic census data in the context of population movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection of facts observed by many persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief need in some research is 'the collection of facts well observed by many persons' and 'each apparent fact should be observed by many'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For certainty, even in matters of fact, agreement of many minds is often needed so that the personal element of each observer may be counteracted. Difficult research benefits from multiple independent observations of the same fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of diverse minds and even dissenting voices
rubrics_metrics.description: On many questions 'minds of all kinds may be well employed', including habitually doubtful persons and those who invent arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity (including doubters and contrarians) helps bring out truth by testing and sharpening it; errors and contrary pleadings can serve to make truth express itself more clearly. Do not exclude heterodox contributors from discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental pliancy and readiness for variation
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic essential to scientific progress is 'mental pliancy and readiness for variation' — the ability to adjust quickly to new conditions of thinking and working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advances change the circumstances of mental life; workers must be able to adopt new methods (e.g., auscultation, numerical methods, evolutionary thinking) or become less useful. Value 'minds that are young, whatever may be their age.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization must be deep, not shallow or self-sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Division into specialties is justified by the increase of knowledge, but the fault of specialism is 'shallowness and the belief in self-sufficiency' with which it is apt to be associated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialists should dig 'deeply' into narrow fields and produce monographs of broad and deep value, yet avoid thinking their specialty is complete or independent of other parts of the science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for periodic conference, mutual criticism, and unity of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers should be 'brought to some consent and unity of purpose' via opportunities for conference, mutual criticism, mutual help, and free discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large international congresses can diminish waste and discord without enforcing uniformity of mind or method; they represent collective consent that different parts of the work are mutually dependent and helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid striving for useless uniformity of mind or method
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should not seek 'a useless and happily impossible uniformity of mind or method'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of purpose should not mean forcing identical thought or method; value diversity while reducing wasteful discord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of truth: adjustment with facts and reasonable beliefs of others
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of truth in every part is 'in the patient and impartial trial of its adjustment with what is true in every other'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge doctrines in isolation; test in the light of facts and reasonable beliefs across disciplines. Be willing to doubt inferences that are inconsistent with others' facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit large-meeting discussion to definite, fact-testable questions
rubrics_metrics.description: In large meetings discussions should be on 'definite questions... which may... be soon brought to the test of fact; there is to be no use of doctrinal touchstones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid debating grand doctrines or party doctrines in large assemblies; prefer questions that can be resolved or advanced by well-directed facts and fair direct inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parties founded on dominant theories or dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties founded on dominant theories have 'always been injurious' in medical sciences, promoting inference over careful observation and repression of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware 'disciples' who adopt a doctrine's name and cease active research. Encourage free research over factional doctrinal loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of careful observation and accurate records
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful observation and records of facts are of primary value; 'Truth so recorded cannot remain barren.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate accuracy and completeness (e.g., in descriptions of the human body) — good recording makes discoveries useful and germinal for future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of apparent errors in advancing truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors and 'contrary pleadings... serve to bring out the truth' and can be useful in a congress context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat all error as merely harmful; examining and disputing errors can clarify and strengthen correct propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of congress: demonstration, diffusion, and invigoration of scientific life
rubrics_metrics.description: The best work of an international congress is 'in the clearing and strengthening of the knowledge of realities' and in bringing 'its force of numbers and varieties of minds to press forward the demonstration and diffusion of truth'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conferences should focus on teaching, learning, discussing, planning research, and forming mutual help and friendships rather than legislating doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: No authoritative prescription of doctrine by congress
rubrics_metrics.description: An international congress should not 'legislate' or declare general doctrines as tests and guides for future study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist attempts by representative bodies to prescribe rigid doctrines; encourage open inquiry and the gradual evolution of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific work should combine novelty, utility, and charity
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical research uniquely combines 'novelty, utility, and charity' — curiosity, practical benefit, and benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for discoveries that are new, useful to others (not merely profit-making), and employed with sympathy, patience, and self-devotion; these three should be kept in balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to human welfare increases with scientific influence
rubrics_metrics.description: As scientific knowledge's influence on moral and social state increases, 'our responsibility will constantly increase' because medicine intimately concerns man's happiness and working power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists should bear in mind the possible impacts of their work on misery, happiness, helplessness, and capacity for work; act with appropriate seriousness and ethical consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be humble about estimating comparative importance of divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not estimate comparatively the importance of different divisions of science; 'we are very imperfect judges of the whole value of any knowledge, or even of single facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that facts may have unknown 'germinal power' and future utility; avoid privileging current practical utility as the sole measure of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: When interpreting census/population data, account for migration and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in colored population growth between censuses often reflect emigration/immigration; e.g., border States added little to colored population due largely to emigration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing demographic percentage gains, consider migration directions, war effects, demand for labor, and local protections that attract populations (illustrated by District of Columbia and Texas/Florida examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider density effects and potential census errors in demographic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually percentage gain lessens as population density increases, but anomalies may occur (e.g., Mississippi and South Carolina had high increases despite density); census anomalies should be scrutinized for prior-census errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept census numbers uncritically; look for anomalies, possible immigration, emigration, and previous census undercounts as explanations.
